details:
Lunanator is a website that helps plan robot missions to the lunar south pole. For 60 candidate landing sites, it shows when the Sun and Earth are actually visible from the ground, taking the surrounding mountains and crater rims into account. It’s live at lunanator.horizonbreachers.workers.dev.

How it works

Sun and Earth positions: NASA/JPL Horizons gives where the Sun and Earth are relative to the Moon, hourly for 5 years (Nov 2026 to Oct 2031).

Terrain: NASA LOLA elevation data is used to trace 360 directions out to 150 km from each site. The highest terrain angle in each direction becomes that site’s skyline.

Visibility: every hour, the Sun or Earth counts as visible when its disc is above the skyline in its direction.

What users can do

Site explorer: pick a site on the south-pole map. You see a 2D sky view of the Sun and Earth over the real skyline, a timeline you can scrub through, and countdowns to the next sunrise, sunset, Earthrise and Earthset.

Mission planner: enter trip dates, how long the robot survives in the dark, and how long it can go without Earth contact. You get ranked sites that fit, plus the top site for sunlight, for Earth link, and for both together.

Robot spec advisor: pick a site and dates. You get the survival time, autonomy, battery size and data storage the robot needs, and the best start dates.

Compare up to three sites side by side, and a Method & accuracy page.

How accurate it is

The Sun and Earth directions matched live JPL Horizons to 0.001° in our spot check.

Compared with NASA’s own illumination maps, the median difference is 4 percentage points for the Sun and 1 for Earth. Sites that differ by more than 20 points are flagged as low confidence.

Rise and set times are approximate, about ±1–2 hours.

Under the hood

It’s a static website with no server of our own. It’s hosted free on Cloudflare, with a small Cloudflare Worker that relays the live JPL check. The data comes from a one-time builder page that turns NASA’s raw data into a single 1.6 MB file.
